1.evidence: Section 2 allows unequal finite populations, ties with being alone, and initially unacceptable partnerships. It defines both moves, specifies which edges survive a switch, and shows why stability requires weakly acceptable current partners and no pair whose members both strictly gain.

2.evidence: In Section 3’s insertion lemma, choosing a most-preferred willing partner confines any new block to the displaced person. Each switch strictly improves one receiving-side member while preserving the others’ positions within the enlarged set, ensuring termination. Section 4 proves the all-single characterization in both directions. Section 5 uses a uniform positive chance of absorption within N−1 steps to establish almost-sure absorption and finite expected time.

3.evidence: Section 4’s one-couple tie shows how an endowed edge can persist even though it cannot form from singles. Section 6 verifies every switch in a four-state cycle and computes how changing the first-meeting probabilities changes the final distribution. Section 7 shows that even positive completion probabilities at every date can leave a positive chance of cycling forever when those probabilities decay.

4.evidence: Section 7 traces both the loss to the abandoned partner and the reversal of the mover’s immediate gain. It identifies the missing inputs for a strategic prediction, including preferences over time and the ability to delay a move. Section 5 specifies how given meeting rates determine absorption probabilities, while Section 7 acknowledges that actual rates and adjustment times remain unknown.

summary: The paper answers how initialization determines reachable stable outcomes and how opportunity selection determines convergence and outcome probabilities. For arbitrary starts, Section 4’s finite graph search is a defensible exact characterization, although it can be costly. The four-state cycle refutes termination along every eligible sequence. Inferring that it also refutes almost-sure absorption under the benchmark would be incorrect, and the manuscript avoids that inference.
